pages.title: Authenticate API requests | Klaviyo Developers
pages.text:
## You will learn

After reading this article, you will be able to distinguish which methods of authentication you should use for making calls with Klaviyo's server- and client-side APIs. You will also learn how to set custom scopes to protect you and your customers’ data.

## Server-side vs client-side APIs

A majority of Klaviyo’s APIs are server-side endpoints, which should be securely handled on your server rather than exposed in the browser. Handle sensitive information via server-side APIs, like bulk-creating events for one or more profiles.

Client-side APIs are used to track and send user behavior data from the client to Klaviyo. They are designed to be called from publicly-searchable, client-side environments only (see Client API reference).

Klaviyo provides 3 methods of authentication including private key authentication and OAuth (used to call server-side APIs) and public key authentication (used to call client-side APIs). Read the table below to learn more about how each method can be used for authenticating API calls:

| Server-side APIs | | Client-side APIs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Private key authentication All /api endpoints use API private keys to authenticate requests. If you do not use an API key for your requests, or if you use a key from the wrong account, your call will return an error. A 401 error indicates an invalid or missing API key. | OAuth If you are a tech partner integrating with Klaviyo, we recommend using OAuth to make authorized API calls. OAuth offers multiple benefits over a private key integration, including security, usability, improved rate limits, and the ability to be listed in Klaviyo's App Marketplace. | Public key authentication All /client endpoints use a public API key: your 6-character company ID, also known as a site ID. We recommend using the Klaviyo object or our Mobile SDKs for interacting with our client-side APIs. |

## Private key authentication

Private API keys can be used to read and write data to your Klaviyo account. Klaviyo allows you to generate multiple private keys for your applications.

### Create a private key

To create a private key:

1. Navigate to your account’s *Settings* page and select **API keys**.
2. Under the *Private API Keys* section, select **Create Private API Key**.

3. Provide a name for your private key and add any of the following scopes:

* Custom Key   
  Allows you to decide how much access to give the third party.
* Read-Only Key   
  Only allows third parties to view all data associated with the endpoint.
* Full Access Key   
  Allows third parties to create, delete, or make changes to anything associated with that endpoint.

4. When you have finished setting your key’s scopes, select **Create**. To protect your account from unauthorized access, you cannot view your private API keys in Klaviyo. After you have created your private API key, copy it to a secure location.

Private keys will have the prefix pk\_ followed by a longer alphanumeric string.

### Use a private key

Private key authentication for `/api` endpoints is performed by setting the following request header:

```
Authorization: Klaviyo-API-Key your-private-api-key
```



curl

```
curl --request GET \
     --url https://a.klaviyo.com/api/{endpoint}/ \
     --header 'Authorization: Klaviyo-API-Key your-private-api-key' \
     --header 'accept: application/json' \
     --header 'revision: 2026-10-15'
```

## Public key authentication

Your 6-character public key, sometimes referred to as a site ID, is a short alphanumeric string that serves as the unique identifier for your Klaviyo account.

Public keys cannot be used to access secure data in your account and are safe to share. Use your public key when you need to track people and events in client-side JavaScript code.

Client-side API calls only require a public API key, also known as a `company_id`, for authentication:

curl

```
curl --request POST \
     --url 'https://a.klaviyo.com/client/subscriptions/?company_id=PUBLIC_API_KEY' \
     --header 'content-type: application/json' \
     --header 'revision: 2026-10-15' \
     --data '
     ...
```

## OAuth

If you're building an app with Klaviyo, use OAuth to provide secure delegated access to users via access tokens (required to enter Klaviyo’s App Marketplace). When setting up OAuth, you must provide designated scopes for each API authorization request you'll want to make.

## Set custom scopes

Setting custom scopes helps you protect your and your customers’ data by limiting what third parties can access. When requesting authorization to make API calls (OAuth), you should only request the scopes required to use your app.

View the API reference documentation to understand which scopes you’ll need to define. For example, if your private key or Klaviyo app needs to create lists, your app needs the `lists:write` scope as shown in the following API reference documentation for the Create List endpoint:

See the full list of scopes needed for each of our APIs below:

**Available scopes for each API**

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| **API endpoint** | **Associated scopes** |
| Accounts | `accounts:read` |
| Campaigns | `campaigns:read` `campaigns:write` |
| Conversations | `conversations:read` `conversations:write` |
| Catalogs | `catalogs:read` `catalogs:write` |
| Coupons | `coupons:read` `coupons:write` |
| Coupon codes | `coupon-codes:read` `coupon-codes:write` |
| Data privacy | `data-privacy:read` `data-privacy:write` |
| Events | `events:read` `events:write` (allows for creating/updating profiles) |
| Flows | `flows:read` `flows:write` |
| Forms | `forms:read` |
| Images | `images:read` `images:write` |
| Lists | `lists:read` `lists:write` |
| Metrics | `metrics:read` `metrics:write` |
| Profiles | `profiles:read` `profiles:write` |
| Push tokens | `push-tokens:read` `push-tokens:write` |
| Reporting | `campaigns:read`  `flows:read` `forms:read`   `segments:read` |
| Reviews | `reviews:read` |
| Segments | `segments:read` `segments:write` |
| Subscriptions | `subscriptions:read` `subscriptions:write` |
| Tags | `tags:read` `tags:write` |
| Templates | `templates:read` `templates:write` |
 Tracking Settings | `tracking-settings:read` `tracking-settings:write` | Web Feeds | `web-feeds:read` `web-feeds:write` |

pages.text:
# Get started with Klaviyo

Get started with Klaviyo's APIs in a few easy steps. Log in, grab your API credentials, and start developing.

## What is Klaviyo?

Klaviyo is a powerful email and SMS marketing tool with a strong commitment to data science. Klaviyo's App Marketplace and API make it simple to build emails and experiences that are truly personal at scale.

> Are you looking to build an integration with Klaviyo and become a partner? Check out our partner resources.

## Take the Klaviyo developer certificate

Kickstart your journey as a Klaviyo developer with the Klaviyo developer certificate. Learn the fundamentals of building with Klaviyo:

* Understand Klaviyo's data model
* Understand our APIs
* Get access to key resources and developer tools
* Explore use cases and examples of building with both server-side and client-side APIs
* Learn how to troubleshoot and handle errors

## Ready to get started?

Welcome to the Developer guides. Follow along the steps below, or select a step to begin, and get started building with Klaviyo today.

* Create a test account (optional)
* Generate sample data
* Install a library (optional)
* Authenticate API requests
* Make a test API request
* Use Klaviyo's Postman collections
* Rate limits & error handling

Then, level up your knowledge with in-depth code guides:

Learn Klaviyo fundamentals with an overview of Klaviyo's data model and architecture:

> Quickstart:
>
> For a step-by-step visual demonstration of how to use Klaviyo APIs, check out our YouTube API tutorial playlist or our Academy guide on connecting your Klaviyo usage with APIs.

## Not a developer?

Head on over to the Help Center to browse a comprehensive collection of how-to's and guides for using Klaviyo products and getting connected to our native integrations. You can also take the <href="https://academy.klaviyo.com/en-us/collections/api-fundamentals-for-marketers" target="\_blank">API fundamentals for marketers learning path to learn more about how to use and troubleshoot Klaviyo's API endpoints.

pages.title: Use Klaviyo's Postman collections | Klaviyo Developers
pages.text:
Postman is a useful web and desktop application for making API calls. Whenever we release an API revision, we update our Postman workspace with a new “collection,” or a group of saved requests to our latest endpoints. In this guide, you will learn how to fork our collections and make API requests in Postman.

## Before you begin

1. Create a Postman account for forking our collections.
2. Create a Klaviyo test account for experimentation purposes. Making API calls with Postman will affect data in your account.
3. Generate sample data in your test account.

## Generate an API key

To test our API calls in Postman, you’ll need a private API key. If you already have one, securely copy it for later use.

1. From your Klaviyo test account’s API keys tab, select **Create Private API Key**. This will prompt you to generate a private API key with full access or a subset of our available scopes.
2. Enter an appropriate name for your key and set your API scopes. For your test account, we recommend creating a full access key to fully experience our APIs.
3. Click **Create**, and securely copy your key for later use.

## Fork our latest Postman collection

You’ll want to test our APIs with our latest Postman collection, as we do not update our older collections.

1. To fork our latest Postman collection, head to our Postman profile.
2. In the *Our content* section, click **View Contents**. This will expand a list of available collections.
3. Scroll to the bottom of the list and click the **Fork** button on the "Latest Stable" collection.

You will be prompted to fork the collection, as shown below:

3. Provide a fork label and select an available workspace from the **Workspace** dropdown. You can always move your forked collection to another workspace for organizational purposes.
4. Click **Fork collection.**

You’ve just added our newest Postman collection to your workspace. Now, you can set up authorization and make Klaviyo API calls in Postman.

## Set up authorization

Once you’ve forked our latest collection, you’ll need to set an API key as the authorization method for each request in the collection. You will learn how to set up a private API key for the full collection, so that you won’t have to set up authorization for each request. You’ll also learn how to test client-side calls with your public API key.

### Authorization with a private API key

1. Ensure that you are in the topmost tab of the collection, e.g., (Stable) Klaviyo API (v2023-10-15), and navigate to the **Authorization** tab in Postman.
2. Hover over `{{privateKey}}`. You will be prompted to provide a value. Paste your copied private API key and select a scope. Save the variable with the enter key.

Now when you click on a specific request, e.g., \*\*Get Events \*\*(within **Events**) and navigate to its **Authorization** tab, the type is automatically set to **Inherit auth from parent**, as shown below.

You can change the type in the *Auth Type* dropdown to **API Key** or select the **Need help authorizing with Klaviyo?** header to override the auth inherited by the collection with a different API key.

### Client-side API calls

Note that you should use klaviyo.js, a JavaScript library fully managed by Klaviyo, for onsite tracking. For mobile use cases, such as creating push tokens, you can call Client API endpoints from our iOS and Android SDKs. You can also use our Client API for client-side applications that require calling our endpoints directly, e.g., creating client subscriptions through a custom form. Check out our documentation for using server-side vs client-side APIs.

Note that when you previously set up authorization for the collection, this did not apply to our client-side API requests. Client-side API calls only require a public API key, also known as a `company_id,` for authentication.

1. From your Klaviyo test account’s API keys tab, copy the public API key at the top of the page.
2. Navigate to a Client API request, e.g., **Create Client Subscription**.
3. Hover over `{{companyId}}`in the request URL. You will be prompted to provide a value. Paste your copied public API key and select a scope in the *Add to* dropdown. We recommend setting the scope to **Global**, so that all collections in your personal Klaviyo workspace can access the shared company ID.

## Navigate your collection

On the left hand sidebar of Postman, you will see all of the available Klaviyo APIs to test. Let’s click on the **Profiles** folder within the collection.

The Profiles API overview on the right includes API’s use cases and considerations. The **Profiles** folder on the sidebar has also been expanded to reveal its sub-folders, **Profiles**, **Bulk Import Profiles**, **Consent**, and **Push Tokens**. Click into these folders to make Profiles API requests.

### Test API call

Let’s make a test API call to **Get Profiles**. First, you can view the supported API reference documentation to the right of your workbench where the request will be sent.

1. Click on the page icon in the top right of the Postman window.

This will open the *Documentation* view, as shown below. This view is useful for referencing allowed fields you can filter or sort responses by and related resources and/or additional fields you can include in your response.

The **Params** tab contains example queries you can make in your request.

2. Select the **filter** param. This will append the filter parameter to the URL with a placeholder `<string>` value, as shown below.

3. In the **Params** tab or in the URL itself, replace `<string>` with a valid field and operator pairing. The example query below fetches profiles created after August 10, 2023.

3. Click **Send**.

The **Body** tab contains the response body, as shown below.

Let’s add a sparse fieldsets query parameter to the request URL to return only specified attributes for profiles, e.g., `created,` in the response and click **Send**:

The final response will look something like this:

Response

```
{
    "data": [
        {
            "type": "profile",
            "id": "01H81WC034AKRMQJQARPEEBHJE",
            "attributes": {
                "created": "2023-08-17T13:53:43+00:00"
            },
            "relationships": {
               ...
            },
            "links": {
                "self": "https://a.klaviyo.com/api/profiles/01H81WC034AKRMQJQARPEEBHJE/"
            }
        },
        {
            "type": "profile",
            "id": "01HD2CCW560NWG693CYF6KF28S",
            "attributes": {
                "created": "2023-10-18T21:52:18+00:00"
            },
            "relationships": {
                ...
            },
            "links": {
                "self": "https://a.klaviyo.com/api/profiles/01HD2CCW560NWG693CYF6KF28S/"
            }
        }
    ],
    "links": {
        "self": "https://a.klaviyo.com/api/profiles/?fields[profile]=created&filter=greater-than(created,2023-08-10T23:00:00Z)",
        "next": null,
        "prev": null
    }
}
```

### Save a request

You can save requests to your Postman collection in its API folder or in a custom folder in your collection.

1. Click on the downward-facing arrow in the top right (next to **Save**), and click **Save as**.
2. Provide a request name, e.g., *Get Profiles Created Date*, and select a folder within the collection, e.g., **Profiles**.
3. Click **Save**. Confirm your request is in the correct folder in the sidebar.

### Copy as code

Postman allows you to copy your requests as code in a supported language of your choice.

1. Click on the code icon in the top right of the Postman window.

This will open the *Code snippet* view, which converts your API request into code, as shown below.

2. Toggle the language in the top left corner if needed. Select the copy icon in the top right corner of the code snippet to copy the code to your clipboard.

## Troubleshoot errors

Postman makes it easy to see your request status. A successful call will typically have a status of 200 (OK) or 202 (Accepted). If you’re encountering a problem when making an API call, check the status code for a hint at the root cause. Below are error statuses you may encounter with troubleshooting tips to help you fix these errors.

### 401 (Unauthorized)

A request that returns a 401 (Unauthorized) error is unverified because authorization credentials are missing or invalid, as shown below. Enter the correct API key and credentials, and try again.

Error

```
{
    "errors": [
        {
            "id": "string",
            "status": 401,
            "code": "not_authenticated",
            "title": "Authentication credentials were not provided.",
            "detail": "Missing or invalid private key.",
            "source": {
                "pointer": "/data/"
            }
        }
    ]
}
```

pages.title: Migrate to OAuth from private key authentication | Klaviyo Developers
pages.text:
## You will learn

If you’re here, it’s likely that your Klaviyo app uses private key authentication. We now require all of our published partners to use OAuth when integrating with Klaviyo. This guide covers how you can migrate and the benefits you’ll get in doing so.

## Why update to OAuth?

Switching your app from private key authentication to OAuth allows for greater exposure to our customers, simpler integration workflows, and access to all new items our R&D team is developing. Here are some benefits you’ll get from the switch:

* **Increased marketplace and in-product visibility**

  Maintain exposure to 150,000+ customers by keeping your app listed and discoverable on the App Marketplace. We expect there to be roughly 5-10x more unique visitors to the App Marketplace due to new improvements.
* **App-branded event metrics**

  Say goodbye to the generic gear icon and get branded exposure on the Klaviyo platform.
* **Seamless integration**

  Streamline the integration process to as little as a few clicks, ensuring a smooth experience for customers, increasing adoption and satisfaction rates.
* **Marketing & enablement opportunities**

  Eligibility for inclusion in marketing newsletters and other enablement initiatives.
* **Exclusive API access**

  Unlock powerful API features, including our Universal Content and Webhooks APIs.

## Migrate to OAuth with an AI agent

## How to migrate to OAuth

If your app was previously published using private key authentication, we estimate that a single engineer will need 1-2 sprints (2-4 weeks) to complete the migration to OAuth. When migrating to OAuth, each step listed below should take roughly 1 week:

1. **OAuth implementation**
   * Create your OAuth app. Please note that after creation, your app will require at least 5 active users to meet our listing requirements before submission.
   * Ensure you properly handle refresh tokens and token expiration.
   * Start completing our Testing & Review Template .
2. **UI and OAuth workflow updates**
   * Update your app’s UI/UX to support connecting to Klaviyo with OAuth.
   * Initiate the OAuth authorization/deny/uninstall flows and eliminate the private key connection option in your app.
   * Ensure that your app meets our app listing requirements**.**
3. **Security and documentation**
   * Complete the security assessment form and address feedback from our Security and Trust team.
   * Create and update help documentation for your app.
   * Set up and use branding for your app metrics.
4. **Review and submission**
   * Review our Pass your app review guide to ensure your app follows best practices.
   * Submit your OAuth app for the Klaviyo team’s approval.
   * Respond and update your app based on Klaviyo review feedback.

## Your fast track migration plan

We've built a working OAuth demo in Flask to help you expedite your migration. Follow the steps below to get started.

### 1. Get your Klaviyo OAuth app credentials

1. Go to your Klaviyo Developer Console
2. Create an OAuth app
3. Add the redirect URL: `http://localhost:5000/auth/callback`
4. Add the following scopes: accounts:read profiles:read
5. Grab your Client ID and Client Secret

### 2. Clone the demo project

First, run the following code to set up your virtual environment.

bash

```
mkdir klaviyo-oauth-demo && cd klaviyo-oauth-demo
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install flask requests python-dotenv
```

You can access the demo Python code here. Save the provided code sample as `oauth_flow.py` and create a `.env.local` file with your credentials:

```
CLIENT_ID=your_client_id_here
CLIENT_SECRET=your_client_secret_here
REDIRECT_URI=http://localhost:5000/auth/callback
KLAVIYO_SCOPES="accounts:read profiles:read"
FLASK_SECRET_KEY=super-secret-for-local-dev  
# Note: for production, do not hardcode FLASK_SECRET_KEY.
# Instead, generate a strong random GUID/hex string and import via a secure env var or secrets manager.
```

### 3. Run the OAuth flow locally

Start the server:

bash

```
python oauth_flow.py
```

Kick off the flow in your browser: `http://localhost:5000/auth/start`

You'll log into Klaviyo, grant consent, and immediately get back your access token and refresh token in JSON.

### 4. Refresh tokens automatically

We've built a `/auth/refresh` endpoint to handle token rotation for you:

bash

```
curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/auth/refresh \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"refresh_token": "YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN"}'
```

This ensures you'll never run into expired token issues.

### 5. Test real Klaviyo API calls

Use the `/whoami` endpoint with your access token to hit Klaviyo's API directly:

bash

```
curl -X GET http://localhost:5000/whoami \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN"
```

This verifies end-to-end that your migration works.

## What this means for your team

* **Engineering leaders:** You don't need to commit weeks of dev time. With our starter code, your teams can cut migration down to a few days.
* **Security & compliance:** OAuth eliminates key sprawl, enables scoped permissions, and simplifies audits.
* **Future-proofing:** This is the industry standard. Your engineers will integrate faster with other modern systems once OAuth is the norm.

## How to productionize your OAuth migration

The demo code gets you from private key → OAuth in minutes. But before rolling this into production, here are the must-dos for a secure, scalable integration:

### 1. Store tokens in your database

Save both the access token and refresh token securely in your database, encrypted at rest. Record `expires_in` (or calculate `expires_at`) so you can proactively refresh before expiry.

### 2. Handle token expiry gracefully

Every Klaviyo API call must include the access token in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header. If you receive a `401 Unauthorized`, your access token has expired. At that point:

1. Use the refresh token to request a new access token
2. Save the new tokens to your DB
3. Retry the original API call transparently

This ensures a seamless experience with no downtime for your users.

### 3. Migrate your existing users

Any users who are using the private key integration will need to re-authenticate using OAuth. Build a simple re-authentication flow into your app to request consent from each user. Once migrated, you can deprecate private key support entirely.

### 4. Metrics auto migration

Good news: any metrics previously tracked via private keys will automatically migrate to branded metrics. This means your data continuity is preserved, and you get all the benefits of OAuth without losing visibility. Learn more about branded metrics here.

# How Klaviyo pricing works: active profiles, sends, and flexible options

Get started with Klaviyo

Set as Preferred Source

Pricing Based on Reachable Customers

Generated by Klaviyo AI

Klaviyo Profile & Email plans are priced by active profiles, with email send capacity included. Month-to-month customers can use billing preferences to accommodate seasonal sending peaks and profile reductions from list cleanup.

* **Active profiles:** Billing is based on reachable contacts, while unsubscribed and suppressed contacts do not count.
* **Email capacity:** Each profile tier includes monthly email send capacity tied to that tier.
* **Flexible sending:** Temporary capacity can cover email or text spikes before returning to the base level next cycle.

Sign upGet a demo

---

Klaviyo prices Profile & Email plans on your active profiles (the customers you can reach) with email send capacity included to match. Profiles are the primary unit, and every plan comes with more send capacity than most brands need, so you can focus on building relationships instead of counting messages. You pay for the audience you reach, not your raw list size.

This page walks through the model the way a docs page would: what counts as an active profile and how send capacity is included, then the flexible options for seasonal peaks and list cleanups, then how a billing cycle plays out, then how to choose the preferences that fit how you send.

Note: These details only apply to month-to-month customers.

## What you're billed for

|  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Unit** | **What it measures** | **What you don't pay for** |
| Active profiles | Contacts you can reach through email, SMS, or other channels | Unsubscribed and suppressed contacts |
| Email sends | Monthly send capacity tied to your plan tier | Sends beyond your tier without a preference set to allow them |
| Text messaging (SMS, MMS, WhatsApp, RCS) | Committed spend on a separate text plan, burned down as you send | Text as part of your email plan, which is billed separately |

Your plan has to cover your active profile count, and send capacity is included with it.

For more information about pricing tiers, check out our pricing page.

## Pricing unit details

### What are “Active profiles”?

Active profiles are the people your brand can actually reach through email, SMS, or other channels. Unsubscribed and suppressed contacts do not count toward billing. Your plan must be profile-compliant. If your active profiles exceed your tier, the account moves to a compliant plan at the next billing cycle.

For example, say you suppress a batch of long-unengaged contacts, and your reachable count drops into a lower tier. Your billable profile base shrinks, especially if you have auto downgrade turned on.

### What are “email sends”?

Klaviyo plans include a monthly email send capacity tied to your tier. With flexible sending on, exceeding that capacity can temporarily give you the next tier's send amount at your current plan's unit rate, then return to base the next cycle. Without flexible sending, upgrade behavior follows the billing preference you selected.

For example, say a brand on a base plan runs a product drop that spikes send volume for one month. With flexible sending on, they flex up for the peak, then return to the base plan automatically at the next cycle.

### What about mobile?

Klaviyo text messaging (SMS, MMS, WhatsApp, and RCS) is separate from your email plan. Rather than a fixed send tier, you commit to an amount of spend based on your expected volume, and it burns down as you send. Rates vary by message type and country: an MMS burns more than an SMS, and each country has its own rate.

Select plans can also flex for spikes. If you burn through your commit, you get a temporary bump to keep sending, then return to your committed level the next cycle — the same idea as flexible sending for email.

For example, a brand with heavy launch-week text bursts could turn on flexible sending for those weeks instead of committing to a higher level of spend they only need a few times a year.

### How to manage your Klaviyo billing preferences

Flexible sending for email or text gives you temporary capacity for peaks, then returns you to base automatically. Auto downgrade on profiles moves your plan down for the next cycle when your active profile count qualifies for a lower tier. Flexible sending and auto downgrade on profiles can run together. Auto downgrade on profiles cannot run alongside auto upgrades based on sends.

For example, say a seasonal sender who cleans the list regularly turns on both flexible sending and auto downgrade, so peak months and list cleanups each show up in the bill correctly.

## How pricing works over a billing cycle

Here’s how these pieces might move across one billing cycle:

1. You start on a base plan sized to your active profiles plus your expected sends.
2. During the cycle, campaigns and flows consume email send capacity, and your profile count rises or falls as you add or suppress contacts.
3. If email sends spike and flexible sending is on, you temporarily get next-tier capacity at your current unit pricing, then snap back to base the next cycle.
4. Near the end of the cycle, profile compliance and, if enabled, auto downgrade are evaluated so the next cycle's plan matches your reachable audience.
5. Between cycles, you aren't forced to stay on a peak plan unless your ongoing profile and send needs actually require it.

**What this means for you:** you pay for reachable profiles and the sending capacity you use. Flexible preferences exist so the bill can track your peaks and your cleanup instead of holding you at your highest-volume month all year.

## How to choose your billing preferences

Match your Klaviyo billing preference to how your platform usage changes throughout the year. If your send volume swings by season, turn on flexible sending. If active profiles drop when you clean the list, turn on auto downgrade.

|  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Preference** | **Best when** | **What happens at peak** | **What happens after list cleanup** |
| Flexible sending (email/text) | Seasonal spikes | Temporary higher capacity, then back to base | No direct effect |
| Auto downgrade on profiles | Active suppression and hygiene | No direct effect | Plan can move to a lower eligible tier |
| Auto upgrade on sends | Steady growth past limits | Plan upgrades | N/A |

### Good rules of thumb to keep in mind:

* If you have mostly seasonal send spikes, turn on flexible sending.
* If you have mostly list cleanup or budget control needs, turn on auto downgrade on profiles.
* If you need both, combine flexible sending and auto downgrade on profiles, not auto upgrade on sends.

### Where to turn this on in Klaviyo:

1. Open your billing settings.
2. Review your recent profile and send usage.
3. Select the preferences that match your pattern.
4. Before a known peak, check the in-product flex-up cost so the bump holds no surprises.

The full steps live in the billing docs.

# How to create or clone a private API key

Estimated 4 minute read

|

Updated Oct 26, 2026, 12:00 AM EST

Owners, Admins, and Managers can create, clone, or delete private API keys.

## You will learn

Learn how to create or clone a private API key and choose scopes that control what an application can access in your Klaviyo account.

Both private API keys and scopes help you protect your and your customers’ data by limiting what third parties can access.

## About private API keys and scopes

An API call lets one application request, add, or edit information in another application.

A private API key identifies your Klaviyo account and authorizes API requests using the scopes assigned to the key. Anyone who has the key can use those permissions, so treat it like a password.

Including a scope for a private API key adds another layer of authorization, limiting what specific elements a third party can access. Scopes are similar to a hotel key, only giving you access to certain areas (like your room or the gym) and not the whole building.

### Scope access levels

When you create a private API key, choose an access level for each API scope. These access levels determine whether a third party can:

* Have no access to the data or actions covered by that scope.
* View data covered by that scope without making changes (read access).
* View data and create, delete, or make other changes covered by that scope (read/write access).

For example, to subscribe profiles to marketing and add them to a Klaviyo list from another application, use Bulk Subscribe Profiles. This endpoint requires `lists:write`, `profiles:write`, and `subscriptions:write`. Granting read/write access for these scopes covers this request; you do not need to grant access to unrelated scopes.

You can learn about Klaviyo’s APIs and see the available scopes for each endpoint on the Developer Portal.

## Before you begin

Please note the following:

* After you create a private API key, you cannot:
  + View the full private API key again after leaving its confirmation page.
    - Tip: securely save private API keys and note down what you want to use them for, such as in a password manager.
  + Add or edit its scopes.
    - If you need different scopes, create a new private API key with the required access. Update any integrations that use the old key and confirm they work before deleting it.
* The creation page starts with **Custom Key** selected. Choose access for at least 1 API scope before creating the key.

If you're not sure which API endpoints, scopes, or permissions you need, please contact a developer or reach out to a Klaviyo partner for help.

## Create a private API key

Treat private API keys like passwords: share them only with parties you trust, and save them in a secure place, such as a vault or password manager. The full key is visible only on the confirmation page immediately after you create it.

1. Click your organization name in the bottom left.
2. Navigate to **Settings**.
3. Click **API keys**.

4. Click **Create Private API Key**.
5. Name the API key.
6. Under **Select Access Level**, choose the access your integration needs:
   * **Read-Only Key**: grants read access for all available API scopes.
   * **Full Access Key**: grants read/write access for all available API scopes.
   * **Custom Key**: lets you choose **No Access**, **Read Access**, or **Read/Write Access** for each row under **API Scopes**. Select access for at least 1 scope.

7. Select **Create**.
8. On the confirmation page, use the copy icon (**Copy Key**) or download icon (**Download (.txt)**) to save the key in a secure place. You cannot view the full key again after leaving this page.
9. Select **Close** to return to **API keys**.

Now, when you share a private API key, the third party will only have access to the information you defined in the scope.

## Clone a private API key

Cloning creates a new private API key using the original key’s scopes. Renamed scopes use their current names, and deprecated scopes without a replacement are omitted.

Note that:

* Cloning does not generate the same key as the original private API key.
* A cloned API key has the same name as the original. You cannot rename it in the API keys settings.

To clone a private API key:

1. Navigate to **Settings > API keys**.
2. Click the 3-dot menu next to the key you want to clone.
3. Select **Clone**, then select **Clone** again in the confirmation dialog.

4. Use the copy icon (**Copy Key**) or download icon (**Download (.txt)**) to save the new key in a secure place, then select **Close**. You cannot view the full key again after closing this page.
5. If you are replacing the original key, update any integrations that use it and confirm they work with the new key. Delete the original only when it is no longer needed.

## Using query parameters

The include parameter adds related data to an API response. The scopes parameter preselects permissions on the private API key creation page. These are separate advanced uses of URL query parameters. If you are unfamiliar with them, work with a developer.

### Include related data in an API response

When an endpoint supports the `include` query parameter, your key needs permission to read both the requested resource and the related data.

For example, `GET /api/profiles/{id}/` retrieves a single profile and requires `profiles:read`. Replace `{id}` with the profile’s ID.

To include that profile’s lists, use `GET /api/profiles/{id}/?include=lists` with both `profiles:read` and `lists:read`. The profiles collection endpoint (`GET /api/profiles/`) does not support including lists.

### Preselect scopes on the creation page

Add the `scopes` query parameter to the private API key creation URL to preselect access levels on the form.

Use a comma-separated list of scope names. Review the selected access, enter a name for the key, and select **Create**. Then copy or download the key before closing the confirmation page.

An example URL is:   
*https://www.klaviyo.com/create-private-api-key?scopes=campaigns:read,campaigns:write*

Navigate to our Developer Portal to see the scopes you can use in this query.

## You will learn

After reading this article, you will be able to distinguish which methods of authentication you should use for making calls with Klaviyo's server- and client-side APIs. You will also learn how to set custom scopes to protect you and your customers’ data.

## Server-side vs client-side APIs

> ## 📘
>
> Check out our video on client- and server-side tracking with Klaviyo's APIs.

A majority of Klaviyo’s APIs are server-side endpoints, which should be securely handled on your server rather than exposed in the browser. Handle sensitive information via server-side APIs, like bulk-creating events for one or more profiles.

Client-side APIs are used to track and send user behavior data from the client to Klaviyo. They are designed to be called from publicly-searchable, client-side environments only (see Client API reference).

Klaviyo provides 3 methods of authentication including private key authentication and OAuth (used to call server-side APIs) and public key authentication (used to call client-side APIs). Read the table below to learn more about how each method can be used for authenticating API calls:

| Server-side APIs | | Client-side APIs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Private key authentication All /api endpoints use API private keys to authenticate requests. If you do not use an API key for your requests, or if you use a key from the wrong account, your call will return an error. A 400 error indicates an invalid or missing API key. | OAuth If you are a tech partner integrating with Klaviyo, we recommend using OAuth to make authorized API calls. OAuth offers multiple benefits over a private key integration, including security, usability, improved rate limits, and the ability to be listed in Klaviyo's App Marketplace. | Public key authentication All /client endpoints use a public API key: your 6-character company ID, also known as a site ID. We recommend using the Klaviyo object or our Mobile SDKs for interacting with our client-side APIs. |

> ## 📘
>
> To manage API keys, you must have an Owner, Admin, or Manager role on your Klaviyo account.

## Private key authentication

Private API keys can be used to read and write data to your Klaviyo account. Klaviyo allows you to generate multiple private keys for your applications.

> ## 🚧
>
> For your account's security, your private API keys should never be used with Client endpoints, exposed in client-side code, or made accessible from public repositories.

### Create a private key

To create a private key:

1. Navigate to your account’s *Settings* page and select **API keys**.
2. Under the *Private API Keys* section, select **Create Private API Key**.

3. Provide a name for your private key and add any of the following scopes:

* Custom Key   
  Allows you to decide how much access to give the third party.
* Read-Only Key   
  Only allows third parties to view all data associated with the endpoint.
* Full Access Key   
  Allows third parties to create, delete, or make changes to anything associated with that endpoint.

> ## 🚧
>
> Note that you cannot add a scope to an existing private key. You also cannot edit a private API key after it’s been created. If you need to remove access to a key based on its current scope, delete it and then create a new key with the correct scope.

4. When you have finished setting your key’s scopes, select **Create**. To protect your account from unauthorized access, you cannot view your private API keys in Klaviyo. After you have created your private API key, copy it to a secure location.

Private keys will have the prefix pk\_ followed by a longer alphanumeric string.

### Use a private key

Private key authentication for `/api` endpoints is performed by setting the following request header:

```
Authorization: Klaviyo-API-Key your-private-api-key
```

```
curl --request GET \
     --url https://a.klaviyo.com/api/{endpoint}/ \
     --header 'Authorization: Klaviyo-API-Key your-private-api-key' \
     --header 'accept: application/json' \
     --header 'revision: 2026-10-15'
```

## Public key authentication

Your 6-character public key, sometimes referred to as a site ID, is a short alphanumeric string that serves as the unique identifier for your Klaviyo account.

Public keys cannot be used to access secure data in your account and are safe to share. Use your public key when you need to track people and events in client-side JavaScript code.

Client-side API calls only require a public API key, also known as a `company_id`, for authentication:

```
curl --request POST \
     --url 'https://a.klaviyo.com/client/subscriptions/?company_id=PUBLIC_API_KEY' \
     --header 'content-type: application/json' \
     --header 'revision: 2026-10-15' \
     --data '
     ...
```

## OAuth

If you're building an app with Klaviyo, use OAuth to provide secure delegated access to users via access tokens (required to enter Klaviyo’s App Marketplace). When setting up OAuth, you must provide designated scopes for each API authorization request you'll want to make.

## Set custom scopes

Setting custom scopes helps you protect your and your customers’ data by limiting what third parties can access. When requesting authorization to make API calls (OAuth), you should only request the scopes required to use your app.

View the API reference documentation to understand which scopes you’ll need to define. For example, if your private key or Klaviyo app needs to create lists, your app needs the `lists:write` scope as shown in the following API reference documentation for the Create List endpoint:
